content: The updated guidelines for the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in pregnant women with HIV-1 infection in the United States include several significant changes and additions. These updates are aimed at improving maternal health and reducing perinatal HIV transmission. 1. Antiretroviral Therapy in Pregnant Women: Recommendations for the use of ARV drugs in pregnant women have been revised to include updated information on drug formulations, dosing, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity during pregnancy. The guidelines now also include the newly approved drug rilpivirine. Tenofovir has been reclassified as a preferred nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) for women co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV). It is now considered an alternative NRTI for other cases. Indinavir and nelfinavir have been moved to the category of protease inhibitors (PIs) to be used only in special circumstances. 2. Preconception Care and Reproductive Options: A new subsection addresses reproductive options for HIV-concordant and serodiscordant couples. This includes discussions on the HPTN 052 trial, which demonstrated that initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) in individuals with CD4 counts between 350 and 550 cells/mm³ significantly reduces the risk of HIV transmission to seronegative partners. The section also discusses trials on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention. 3. Infant Prophylaxis: The guidelines now recommend a two-drug regimen for infant prophylaxis in cases where mothers did not receive antepartum ARV drugs. This regimen includes zidovudine for six weeks combined with three doses of nevirapine during the first week of life. This approach is preferred due to its lower toxicity compared to a three-drug regimen. For full-term infants, the recommended dose of zidovudine for post-exposure prophylaxis is 4 mg/kg orally twice daily for six weeks, starting as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 6–12 hours of delivery. 4. Breastfeeding and HIV: Breastfeeding is not recommended for HIV-infected women in the United States, even for those receiving combination ART, due to the availability of safe and feasible alternatives. 5. HIV and Hepatitis B Co-Infection: All pregnant women with HIV/HBV co-infection should receive a combination ARV regimen that includes drugs active against both HIV and HBV. The preferred dual NRTI backbone is tenofovir plus either lamivudine or emtricitabine. 6. Acute HIV Infection in Pregnancy: A new section has been added to address the diagnosis and management of acute HIV-1 infection during pregnancy. 7. HIV-2 Infection in Pregnancy: A new section discusses the diagnosis and management of HIV-2 infection in pregnant women. 8. Postpartum Care: Expanded discussions include considerations for discontinuing ARV drugs postpartum, counseling on safer sex practices, and contraception during the postpartum period. 9. International Clinical Trials: Recent results from international clinical trials, such as HPTN 046 and NICHD-HPTN 040/PACTG 1043, are included. These trials demonstrated the efficacy of extended infant nevirapine prophylaxis in reducing postnatal infections and the benefits of combination infant ARV prophylaxis in reducing intrapartum transmission when mothers did not receive antepartum ARV drugs. 10. Guidelines Development and Evidence: The guidelines are based on scientific evidence and expert opinion, with recommendations graded according to the strength of the recommendation and the quality of evidence. Updates are made regularly to reflect new data, drug approvals, and safety information. 11. Global Considerations: While these guidelines are designed for use in the United States, alternative strategies may be appropriate in other countries depending on local resources, availability of ARV drugs, and breastfeeding practices. 12. Mechanisms of ARV Prophylaxis: ARV drugs reduce perinatal HIV transmission through multiple mechanisms, including lowering maternal viral load, providing pre-exposure prophylaxis to the infant via placental transfer, and post-exposure prophylaxis after birth. These updates aim to provide healthcare providers with the most current and evidence-based recommendations for managing HIV in pregnant women and preventing mother-to-child transmission.
